slides.title: One trusted online store.
slides.text: Imagine opening one online store and finding a small collection that feels chosen, rather than accumulated. Different clothing labels, brought together by a clear point of view. Pieces you want to wear, useful comparisons, and honest explanations of the evidence behind them. That is the idea: our brand is the store. Initially, the clothes belong to existing labels and keep their names. We would sell a considered selection for our market, not simply send visitors elsewhere. Start with a compelling online collection, then earn the right to grow.

slides.title: Less searching. Better choosing.
slides.text: The customer should not need fifteen browser tabs to make one good choice. Fit information lives in one place, delivery conditions somewhere else, and ethical claims can be difficult to compare. Our hypothesis is that a well-edited store can reduce that work without hiding the differences between labels. Start with style, fit and the full delivered price. Let customers open the supporting evidence when they want more depth. This is a proposition to test with Icelandic shoppers, not an established finding about what they will buy.

slides.title: A local-access opportunity. To test.
slides.text: The opportunity is not that Iceland has no good clothing shops. It is that some useful labels may be hard for our intended customer to discover or buy conveniently. A locally relevant online collection could help those labels reach that customer, while making comparisons and service clearer. We still need to map existing stockists, cross-border options and delivered prices. Distribution territories and permission to resell also need checking. Local access is the hypothesis. A population count is not a demand forecast, and interest alone will not establish a viable business.

slides.title: Our store. Their labels.
slides.text: Think of two layers of brand. The clothing label tells you whose garment it is. Our store supplies the edit: which pieces belong together, how they are presented, and why they deserve a place in this collection. That distinction is fundamental. We are not launching garments made for us, and we are not building just a directory of links. The intended revenue comes from product sales. Exactly who operates checkout and carries the merchant responsibilities remains to be decided. An own-label range could be a later option, after demand, evidence and operations are proven.

slides.title: Real labels. Not agreed suppliers.
slides.text: Two existing labels make the idea tangible. In the October twenty-seventh snapshot, Yes Friends listed its Original T-shirt at twelve to fourteen pounds. Its ethics explanation describes contributing towards a living wage; that is a company claim about a mechanism, not proof of full wage coverage. Honest Basics listed its Basic T-shirt at fourteen euros ninety, declaring seventy percent organic and thirty percent recycled cotton. These are foreign consumer listings, not our prices or wholesale quotes. Both are research examples, not confirmed suppliers, approved distribution partners or evidence that Iceland lacks stockists.

slides.title: The first edit, on screen.
slides.text: Here is the visual-merchandising opportunity, translated into a webshop. Give the collection a clear mood, a useful colour story and a deliberate product hierarchy. Keep each clothing label visible. Let customers compare fit and fabric, then filter the information by evidence status: what the brand reports, what is independently checked, and what remains unknown. The illustrated collection is a design study, not real available stock. Its job is to show how retail judgement could make a mixed-label range feel coherent, without pretending that every label has the same evidence or that better layout already means more sales.

slides.title: Follow one real product.
slides.text: Now move from the imagined collection to one real research example: the Honest Basics Basic T-shirt. Its product listing declares a seventy-thirty blend of organic and recycled cotton and a relaxed fit. Those are useful starting points, clearly labelled as brand reported. Our current record does not establish batch-level chain of custody, a verified wage outcome, or our right to sell it in Iceland. A good evidence panel makes those gaps visible beside what is known. It does not turn an attractive product page or a material claim into a blanket ethical endorsement.

slides.title: Clicks are not orders.
slides.text: An experienced retailer will ask whether the edit earns its keep. Compare a standard layout with an evidence-led collection treatment, holding product, price, availability and traffic as comparable as possible. Count completed purchases, not button clicks. Then examine basket value, refunds, returns and contribution from a mature order cohort. Before lawful trading is ready, interviews and selection tests can teach us about preferences, but they are not sales conversion. Once real orders exist, show the denominators and uncertainty. The objective is kept sales at workable cost, not a flattering dashboard.

slides.title: Choose the route before the promise.
slides.text: Probably no initial stock is a starting preference, not a fulfilment agreement. We should compare commercially viable routes before choosing one. Small-stock wholesale gives more handling control but ties up cash. Preorders need credible availability, delivery promises and refund arrangements. Supplier fulfilment may reduce stockholding, but depends on a supplier actually supporting our territory and service requirements. Consignment also requires an agreement; it is not automatically available. We do not need to commit to all these routes. We need one that works for the customer, the label and the business before accepting an order.

slides.title: Product sales. Real costs.
slides.text: The revenue model is product sales, not an invented affiliate commission. But fewer boxes in our possession would not mean cost-free margin. Start with actual sales revenue after refunds, treated correctly for value added tax. Subtract product cost, freight, fulfilment, payment charges, return handling and variable service or acquisition costs. Include costs incurred on refunded orders too. Then fund systems, research and the team's work before calling anything profit. No supplier quote supports a margin number yet. The useful next spreadsheet compares agreed routes and real costs, including cash timing, rather than borrowing economics from a bulk-stock scenario.

slides.title: No order before the gates.
slides.text: Before a customer can buy, the operational promises have to be real. Confirm the labels and resale permissions, distribution territory, samples and evidence. Get written commercial terms and establish who takes payment, issues the invoice and owns each customer obligation. Confirm Iceland shipping costs, delivery times, import and value added tax treatment, plus the returns address and refund process. Supplier fulfilment would not make these questions disappear. Customer-facing information needs appropriate Icelandic review and lawful terms. These are decision gates, not paperwork to finish after launch, and none is presented as already approved.

slides.title: A narrow catalogue. A real test.
slides.text: The first pilot is a narrow branded online collection, not a predetermined stock purchase. Choose a customer and a small, coherent edit. Check label access, product quality, evidence and commerce terms before taking orders. Use early customer tests to learn about selection, fit information and price; do not count those responses as revenue. If the commercial and legal gates pass, test actual selling within an agreed cash and loss cap. Reconcile returns and all costs before expanding. There is no arbitrary unit-buy promise or six-week victory condition. Continue, revise or stop on the evidence.

slides.title: Two crafts. One online experience.
slides.text: The partnership opportunity is retail judgement working with technical leverage. Retail brings range selection, styling, visual hierarchy, fit knowledge and an understanding of why customers hesitate. Technology brings usable commerce, readable evidence and measurements that connect the collection to actual orders and costs. Neither side substitutes for the other. A polished interface cannot choose a convincing range by itself, and an inspiring edit still needs reliable operations. These are proposed contributions, not appointments or agreed workloads. Design the first collection together, then agree responsibilities, commercial decisions and how the partnership would work.

slides.title: Let’s design the first online collection.
slides.text: Return to that opening screen: one trusted store, selected labels, clearer choices. The ambition is to make discovery feel good and buying feel understandable, while giving worthwhile existing labels a route into our market. The next step is concrete. Choose the customer. Sketch the first online collection. Decide which labels to investigate and what evidence and service would be good enough. Then see whether actual terms and unit economics justify trading. An own-label line can remain a future possibility, not a condition for starting. For now, let us make the first edit worth choosing.
